body.text: Treasurer Jim Chalmers says conflict in the Middle East is making Australia's inflation challenge worse and says the budget is not the primary driver of prices.
Meanwhile, Australia and Solomon Islands have signed a "historic" treaty that Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says will strengthen shared prosperity and security.

Deal done: Greens to support trust tax
Another deal has been struck: the Greens have agreed to support Labor's changes on discretionary trusts.
In return for supporting a 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts, the Greens say the government have agreed to cut tax breaks for private jet fuel.

"We have forced the government to come to an arrangement where those ultra wealthy, when they're flying around the country in their private jets, whether it's Gina Rinehart or Clive Palmer or Pauline Hanson, are now going to be paying the same effective rate for when they fill up their tanks, as ordinary Australians do in a cost of living crisis," Shoebridge says.
Coalition vows to repeal digital duty of care
After being somewhat non-committal this morning, the Coalition has confirmed it: they'll repeal the digital duty of care bill if elected.
Shadow Communications Minister Sarah Henderson called the legislation "deeply regressive" and a "blank cheque for political censorship".

"We fear Labor’s digital duty of care will be virtually impossible to comply with given the dangerously vague and subjective definitions of harm. Labor is walking blindly into a legal nightmare of protracted investigations, costly litigation, and regulatory uncertainty," she says in a statement.

"The Coalition strongly supports effective remedies for victims of serious online harm, but a legal reform of this magnitude cannot be the product of policy on the run."The Coalition rejects the false choice between keeping children safe online and defending free speech."We will hold big tech to account, strengthen online safety laws, and defend the democratic freedoms of Australians."
"The Coalition strongly supports effective remedies for victims of serious online harm, but a legal reform of this magnitude cannot be the product of policy on the run.
"The Coalition rejects the false choice between keeping children safe online and defending free speech.
"We will hold big tech to account, strengthen online safety laws, and defend the democratic freedoms of Australians."
Wilson says govt is being 'defeated by inflation'
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson says the federal government and treasurer are being "defeated by inflation".
The Liberal frontbenchers says he's concerned unemployment has increased to 4.9 per cent, ahead of Reserve Bank forecasts.
He says the government doesn't understand they are behind the rise in inflation to 4.9 per cent in October.
Wilson says its "destroying confidence and hope" in the economy.
"At every point, your job is to defeat inflation. Instead, the treasurer is being defeated by inflation and the Albanese government is being defeated by inflation," Wilson says.
Shadow treasurer dismisses treasurer's argument about conflict and inflation
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson has again dismissed the treasurer's argument that war in the Middle East isn't helping Australia's inflation challenge.
Earlier, Jim Chalmers told the media that while the country was struggling with inflation before the Middle East war, the conflict was making it worse.
But the shadow treasurer says inflation is a home-grown challenge.

"The underlying inflation that Australia is experiencing that's leading to interest rate hikes went above the target in July of 2025, a full seven months before a single bomb was dropped on Tehran and it's continued to rise since," Wilson says.
Asked if the increase in inflation was behind the rise in right-wing parties, Wilson says inflation "always creates problems around social division".
Wilson 'highly suspicious' of Labor's interest in reducing spending
The shadow treasurer says he's "highly suspicious" the federal government has any interest in reducing spending.
Tim Wilson says the Coalition has outlined more than $31 billion worth of savings, which would target climate initiatives, the National Reconstruction Fund, the NDIS and illicit tobacco.
The mid-year fiscal and economic outlook is approaching, and the shadow treasurer says the government's focus should be on cutting spending.

"The problem with the Albanese government is they have become completely disinterested in the consequences of their active inflation agenda," Wilson says."And we're seeing it. Australians are living it. They are paying higher prices in interest rates."
"The problem with the Albanese government is they have become completely disinterested in the consequences of their active inflation agenda," Wilson says.
"And we're seeing it. Australians are living it. They are paying higher prices in interest rates."
Wilson says CPI figures show inflation is 'persistent and challenging'
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson has just stepped for his press conference here in Canberra to discuss inflation.
Inflation rose half a per cent in October, in original terms, with the annual rate of inflation lifting to 4.9 per cent.
Wilson says today's figures show how "persistent and challenging" Australia's inflation is.

"We have persistent government inflation, driven inflation by spending and the treasurer keeps putting his foot down on the accelerator by continuing to stoke and spending as part of his active inflation agenda," Wilson says.
The shadow treasurer says Australia needs a change of economic model that improves economic growth.
Negotiations over trusts taxes ongoing: Chalmers
We're no closer to a deal between the Greens and Labor on discretionary trusts.
The government wants to impose a 30 per cent minimum tax on the trusts. But it's yet to win over the minor party over concerns the exemption for charitable giving is too broad.
Chalmers says discussions are ongoing, adding the Greens are negotiating in good faith.
"I've learned not to take any outcome in the Senate for granted until it happens," he says.
The treasurer also welcomed the deal struck between Labor and the Greens earlier today on changes to the private health insurance rebate.
Chalmers again flags public service cuts ahead of MYEFO
Last night, Treasurer Jim Chalmers sat down in the ABC studio and flagged the public service could face cuts in the Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook.
So what does he mean when he talks about finding efficiencies in public service spending?
Of course, he doesn't go into specifics. Instead, he points to the decisions already taken (reducing the use of consultants) but says there's still "more work to do".
Asked if that would include a public-service-wide efficiency dividend or a broader uptake in AI adoption, Chalmers repeats the position hasn't been finalised.
"I'm reluctant to be more specific," he says but adds the APS has a lot of opportunities.
Chalmers defends record and earlier electricity and fuel subsidies
Australia's 4.9 per cent inflation rate puts us well ahead of other nations like Canada and the UK (3.1 per cent and 3.6 per cent).
So what are the factors making Australia's battle with inflation worse?
Treasurer Jim Chalmers says our economy has been "a bit stronger" than some other nations.
"We've had lower unemployment than some of those countries. We've got the second fastest growth. If you compare us to the G7, the only economy with faster growth than us is the US," he says.
So is inflation the cost of having a good economy? Chalmers doesn't agree to that.
He says the private sector recovery was "quicker and stronger" than people thought it would be and the Middle East war hasn't helped matters.

A reporter then asks if the government made a mistake by responding to inflation spikes with electricity and fuel rebates, and whether the best cost-of-living relief would've been to just prepare the nation for hard choices to come.
"No," Chalmers responds.
"I think those policies were an important part of us helping to take the sting out of this higher inflation," he says.
Chalmers again urges people not to pretend that global pressures were not at play, and that private demand had tripled while public spending halved.
Does Chalmers regret declaring last year that inflation battle was behind us?
Treasurer Jim Chalmers acknowledges the Australian economy is facing a "very serious" moment.
"We will respond in substantial ways," he says.
"It is the case that our economy, our people and certainly their government are grappling with a complex combination of pressures and the statement that we release in December does reflect that."
Chalmers is asked if he regrets a 2025 declaration that the inflation battle was behind us. He stands by it.
"That's a factual statement. The worst of the inflation was in 2022 in the year that we came to office," he says, before digging into the Coalition for having "no savings" in their last budget.
Pressed further about whether that's a like for like comparison, Chalmers says yes.
"I think if you're prepared to accept and acknowledge the global factors in 2022, it's important that you accept and acknowledge global factors in 2026."
No quick fixes for inflation challenge: Chalmers
Treasurer Jim Chalmers is asked how he can assure further spending promises won't make the inflation challenge worse.
He points to the cost-of-living relief the government confirmed earlier in the week, when it confirmed the extension of the PBS-listed medicines price freeze.
But he says there is no amount of spending or saving that make "the inflation challenge go away overnight".
"That's because it has a number of drivers, primarily in this case, automotive fuel," he says.
But Chalmers doesn't agree with a reporter's suggestion the government hadn't yet made "hard decisions" to bring down spending.
"We've been making hard decisions for four and a half years," he says, adding there will be net saves in the mid-year budget update.
Middle East conflict 'making inflation challenge worse'
Treasurer Jim Chalmers has just stepped up for his press conference.
He's responding to the news inflation jumped to 4.9 per cent to the year in October.
Chalmers says the primary driver of the "unwelcome" uptick was the "flow through from global oil prices to petrol bowsers".
The treasurer says while Australia was already struggling with inflation before the Middle East war, the conflict "was making it much worse".
But he says the budget is not the "primary driver of prices in our economy".
BBC's Bluey ban on Christmas float is 'bloody outrageous', pollies say
Australian politicians have said the BBC's intervention in a South Australian town's Christmas parade is "bloody outrageous".

The BBC wrote a cease-and-desist letter to a Mount Gambier real estate company, telling them to remove Bluey-themed costumes and float from their annual community parade, citing copyright infringement.
"I think BBC could have a bit more Christmas spirit," Communications Minister Anika Wells said.
In a rare moment of consensus between the leaders of the Nationals and the Greens, both Matt Canavan and David Shoebridge criticised the move.
"I'll get in contact with the BBC again about this. This is ridiculous, and there should be just fair use of copyright in these sort of instances," Canavan said on Today.
"It's bloody outrageous that the BBC is saying to Mount Gambier, you can't have Bluey on a float," Shoebridge added.
"I'm all for nationalising Bluey. Bring it back into Australian ownership and sod off the BBC."
Both Canavan and Shoebridge slammed the ABC's deal with the BBC over the beloved cartoon dog, which gave the BBC global distribution and merchandising rights.
Wells, who is also sports minister, added she was well acquainted with BBC rights issues, as she wanted Bluey to be a mascot for the Brisbane 2032 Olympics.
Inflation figures 'unwelcome but unsurprising': Chalmers
Jim Chalmers has just released a statement responding to the October inflation figures. Inflation jumped up to 4.9 per cent in the year to October, up from 4.3 per cent in September.
"This is another unwelcome but unsurprising reminder of the pressure Australians are under," the treasurer said.
"October saw inflation rise in most major advanced economies and interest rates are going up around the world as a result.

"Since September, every major advanced economy has had a rate rise, and the market is pricing further rate hikes in every one of them. Inflation is still much lower than its peak in 2022 but it’s still too high.
"We had an inflation challenge in our economy before the conflict in the Middle East but the war is making it worse.
"This inflation challenge is the primary influence on the budget update we will finalise in the coming weeks and release in December."
Coalition won't support over-65s private health rebate changes despite carve-out
The Coalition has welcomed the government's changes to its bill to wind back the over-65s private health insurance rebate, but says it still won't support the policy.
Labor has caved to Greens pressure and agreed to carve out pensioners from its bill to wind back the over-65s private health insurance rebate and get it passed through parliament.
If the bill passed unamended, it would have raised about $3 billion which Labor says would have been reinvested into the aged care sector.
Shadow Health Minister Anne Ruston says the Coalition welcomes the change, but still won't support the policy because carving out pensioners doesn't go far enough.

"We're pleased that the government has backfliped today but this backflip, by carving out pensioners, does not fix what we think is fundamentally a bad policy," Ruston says."A bad policy because it's going to still impact older Australians who have paid private health insurance all of their lives."
"We're pleased that the government has backfliped today but this backflip, by carving out pensioners, does not fix what we think is fundamentally a bad policy," Ruston says.
"A bad policy because it's going to still impact older Australians who have paid private health insurance all of their lives."
Independent MP Monique Ryan says she'll support Labor's amendments. She says more aged care beds and support for elderly Australians shouldn't be at the expense of the private health rebate.
Tasmanian senator Jacqui Lambie has urged the government not to seek savings from elderly Australians, and has urged Labor to "go after" their donors instead.
Independent MP Kate Chaney says while the federal government needs to find savings, pensions "are not the place to start".
Inflation jumps to 4.9 per cent in the year to October
That's up from 4.3 per cent in September. Housing, fuel and electricity prices have driven inflation higher in the last 12 months.
We're expecting Treasurer Jim Chalmers to stand up in about an hours' time to respond to the inflation data. We'll bring you that live in the federal politics blog.
But if you're looking to get down into the nitty-gritty, our friends over at the business blog have you covered.
Key Event
Marles apologises to current and former defence personnel over homosexuality ban
The defence minister has offered an apology to ADF personnel and veterans over a ban on homosexuality, that he has described as a "shameful chapter" in Australia's military history.
The ban was in place until 1992 when it was lifted under the former Keating government, and any defence personnel found to be gay or lesbian could be sacked.
In a speech to parliament this morning Richard Marles apologised on behalf of the Australian government, and with the chief of the defence force.
"For the surveillance, and the fear you lived under, we are sorry. For the interrogations, and for being asked to betray your mates, we are sorry," he said.

"For the careers ended and the promises wasted, we are sorry. For discharge papers that told lies about your service, we are sorry."For the years you felt unwelcome amongst your fellow veterans, we are sorry. To the families who never knew why, and to the families who knew and grieved, we are sorry."And for the thirty-four years it has taken us to say so, we are sorry."
"For the careers ended and the promises wasted, we are sorry. For discharge papers that told lies about your service, we are sorry.
"For the years you felt unwelcome amongst your fellow veterans, we are sorry. To the families who never knew why, and to the families who knew and grieved, we are sorry.
"And for the thirty-four years it has taken us to say so, we are sorry."

Marles acknowledged Chief Petty Officer Anita van Der Meer, who took her case to the Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission in 1992 while facing dismissal from the ADF due to her same-sex relationship, and was present in the gallery.
Key Event
Applause in Senate as digital duty of care bill passes
As expected, the digital duty of care bill has breezed through the Senate, with amendments.
Those in favour of the bill broke out into applause when Senate president Sue Lines confirmed consideration of the bill had concluded.
Communications Minister Anika Wells watched on as the votes were taking place and shared a hug with Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young afterwards.
The bill will now go back to the House where MPs will need to rubber-stamp the amendments. That will also pass easily, given Labor's majority.
Key Event
📷 Albanese and Wale sign new Australia-Solomon Islands treaty
Wale says he welcomes another motion of no confidence
Solomon Islands PM Matthew Wale has been asked about a motion of no confidence he faced in his nation's parliament earlier this year which failed.
Wale has defended the signing of the treaty with Australia, saying the decision to sign it was taken by his caucus and entire cabinet.
He says he welcomes another motion of no confidence. In fact, he says he looks forward to it.
"There was unanimity, to sign and so that's what we've done. I welcome another motion of no confidence. I look forward to it," Wale says.
And that's where we'll leave that press conference with Albanese and Wale.
Key Event
Coalition tries, and fails, to delay digital duty of care passage
While the blog's focus has been on the PM's press conference, the Coalition was trying to wrangle up some Senate shenanigans.
The final stages of the digital duty of care bill were due to kick off just after 10am and because of the deal struck between the government and the Greens, it's passage is all but confirmed.
But that didn't stop Shadow Communications Minister Sarah Henderson from doing her best to try and send the bill off to another inquiry. It would have delayed its passage until next year.

The Greens voted with government to shut the move down. The chamber quickly moved on to dealing with the bill. Henderson got up for a second time, moving a suspension of standing orders (aka the business of the day) so the bill could be debated for as long as needed.
If agreed to, the Coalition could've used it to run out the clock and delay its passage until later.

Labor and the Greens voted together to shut that down. So we're officially now in voting time. There are a number of amendments to get through here, so if you're in Parliament House expect the bells to be ringing on and off for a little while.
Key Event
Treaty would require SI to 'consult' with Australia on non-PIF related developments: PM
The Australian PM has been asked about a clause in the treaty signed today which guarantees the Pacific island nation's sensitive infrastructure will remain free of militarisation.
Anthony Albanese has been asked if there's a commitment by Solomon Islands to consult on any decision around national security with Australia.
The Australian prime minister says the treaty provides to "deepen dialogue and cooperation" on security and critical infrastructure.
He confirms the treaty would require Solomon Islands to consult with Australia on critical infrastructure and national security developments related to non Pacific Island Forum (PIF) members.

"That's consistent with the view that we have that the priority for security cooperation comes from PIF members and it states very clearly that Australia remains the Solomon Islands security partner of choice," Albanese says.
Wale won't discuss details of China treaty due to non-disclosure clause
Solomon Islands PM Matthew Wale has been asked by reporters about the status of a treaty between Solomon Islands and China.
As we've reported, Solomon Islands is set to scrap a controversial security treaty signed with China in 2022.
The treaty allowed China to rotate its police training teams in Solomon Islands, with about two dozen permanent Chinese police in the country at one time.
Foreign Minister Penny Wong has previously called the agreement, signed under the former Morrison government, Australia's "worst foreign policy blunder in the Pacific since the end of World War II".
Wale says he can't speak about the treaty because it contains a non-disclosure clause.
"We have ongoing discussions with China. But today is about our relationship with Australia and the treaty we have signed today," Wale says.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese makes the point the government will be releasing the treaty "fully and transparently".
Key Event
Solomon Islands PM says treaty 'elevates' relationship with Australia
Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale says the new treaty with Australia resets and elevates the bilateral relationship.
Wale says his country has been a source of doubt and uncertainty in the Pacific region for a number of reasons.
"Those days are done. Gone. We don't want to be there again," Wale says.
"That comes by being trusted by our neighbours and it is important to not only Australia and New Zealand of course, and the entire Pacific Islands region."
Key Event
PM Albanese confirms new major treaty with Solomon Islands
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Solomon Islands PM Matthew Wale have just stepped up for their press conference in Canberra.
Albanese has confirmed Australia and Solomon Islands will be signing a "historic" treaty that he says will strengthen shared prosperity and security.
The PM says as part of the treaty, Australia will help strengthen Solomon Islands's police force, improve the Pacific nation's border security and deliver support to provide free education.
It will also create opportunities for Solomon Islanders to come to Australia, Albanese says, to work in aged care and childcare.

"When our neighbours are stronger, our region is stronger. Backing our Pacific neighbours is an investment in Australia's own security and our own prosperity," Albanese says."This treaty will strengthen our security partnership. Australia is proud to be the Solomon Islands main security partner.
"When our neighbours are stronger, our region is stronger. Backing our Pacific neighbours is an investment in Australia's own security and our own prosperity," Albanese says.
"This treaty will strengthen our security partnership. Australia is proud to be the Solomon Islands main security partner.
Albanese has thanked Wale for the "courage" of his leadership which he says has taken the bilateral relationship to the next level.
Key Event
Deal done: Pensioners to be carved out from private health insurance rebate change
Breaking into our coverage of the Solomon Islands PM presser to bring you the latest:
Health Minister Mark Butler has confirmed he's done a deal with the Greens to pass its proposed change to the private health insurance rebate.
The government wanted to wind back the rebate Australians aged 65 and over received on their cover, banking $3 billion over four years to be spent elsewhere in the aged care sector.

It's fair to say the proposal initially was pretty friendless, and the Greens voted with the Coalition and the rest of the crossbench to strike the bill off the agenda completely in the last joint sitting fortnight.
The minor party wanted pensioners carved out from the changes. Butler confirms he's now agreed to that demand after it became clear there was no pathway for the bill in the Senate.
It means the government will forgo half of the expected savings from the change. But Butler says the promised $3b will still be put aside for aged care.

"It was intended that government would invest the $3 billion saved through this measure to deliver more residential aged care beds, more Support at Home Packages, shorter wait times and better care for older Australians. The full investment into aged care announced in the budget will continue," he says.
"The government also recognises the realities of the Senate, and reaching agreement was necessary to secure passage of the bill and deliver these important investments into aged care."
Albanese and Solomon Islands PM to speak shortly
Hello friends! I'm jumping on the blog to take you through a press conference with Anthony Albanese and Solomon Islands PM Matthew Wale happening any moment now.
We expect Albanese and Wale to announce the signing of a major new treaty with the Pacific island nation at this press confernece.
As we've reported, Wale was welcomed to Parliament House this morning with a 19-gun salute and military guard.
Stand by! We'll bring you that press conference as soon as it happens!
Union pushes to force data centre developers to train more electricians

Data centre builders would be forced to train their own sparkies to prevent the AI boom from draining electricians from housing and renewable energy projects, under a plan being pushed by union and industry groups.

The joint proposal from the National Electrical and Communications Association (NECA) and the Electrical Trades Union (ETU) would require developers to take on more first-year apprentices rather than poaching already qualified electricians and later-stage apprentices from other work sites.
Developers would be required to act as "anchor host employers", with a mandated ratio of one apprentice for every three trade workers in the construction phase of a data centre.
The plan would also make developers help fund additional TAFE and VET places via a levy, with the NECA and ETU arguing taxpayers should not bear the full cost of training additional workers.
The groups want the requirements baked into the government's National AI Framework, which is expected to be brought before parliament in the new year.
📸 Matthew Wale arrives at Parliament House
Wale welcomed to Parliament House with 19-gun salute
If you're in Canberra and wondering what that big boom just was, have no fear, it was just the ceremonial welcome for Solomon Islands PM Matthew Wale.
He was welcomed with a 19-gun salute and a military guard to honour his arrival at Parliament House.
As friend of the blog Stephen Dziedzic has been reporting this morning, Wale is in Canberra ahead of the expected signing of a treaty with Australia.
📸Anika Wells's busy morning on the victory lap
The ABC's Matt Roberts is always watching.
What does the treaty mean for the Solomon Islands' security deal with China?
Just returning briefly to the Solomon Islands–Australia treaty set to be signed this morning.

While there will be lots of attention on the terms of the treaty, expect Matthew Wale to also field questions from the press on another pact: the contentious 2022 security agreement with China, which now looks to be on the chopping block.
Yesterday the ABC confirmed that Wale's government recently informed China it doesn't intend to renew the pact when it comes up for renewal in April next year.

If Solomon Islands sticks with that commitment, it will represent a significant foreign policy victory for the government, which has been trying to roll back China's policing presence across the Pacific.
But expect both leaders to tread delicately on the subject this morning, with Solomon Islands trying to avoid deeply alienating Beijing.
The federal government has already been signalling that tearing up the China pact wasn't a pre-condition for signing the Australia-Solomon Islands treaty.
After all, Wale has long been sceptical of China playing a security role in Solomon Islands, even before these negotiations kicked off.
But the two announcements both show the same direction of travel.
Wale seems to be making it clear that he'll turn to Australia and its traditional partners for security assistance — while still maintaining strong development and commercial ties with Beijing.
Labor 'crab-walking away' from data centre renewables-only power edict: Hastie
A bipartisan joint committee handed down 46 recommendations on AI, including establishing an independent body to oversee the technology and creating national consistent standards.
But while the committee agreed data centres must bring their own power, it didn't reach consensus on the extent the government should "specify" the energy source requirements.
The government has previously issued a renewables-only edict.
But Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie is questioning whether Labor is "slowly crab-walking" away from that.
"I think they're realising that AI is energy intensive," he tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast.
"We have an abundance of natural resources here that could power the AI revolution and that's why the committee was ultimately agnostic on power sources.
"But I think ultimately if people want to build AI they need to build more energy into the grid so that it doesn't compromise regular Australians and their security when it comes to power."
While the report itself didn't reach consensus, additional comments provided by Labor reiterated "renewables supported by storage is the lowest cost to power AI infrastructure".
Coalition will 'work through' whether it'll vow to repeal digital duty of care
Angus Taylor has declined to say whether a future Coalition government would repeal the digital duty of care legislation.
The bill, which is expected to pass parliament today, would put the onus on big tech to prevent foreseeable harms. The Coalition is vehemently opposed to the laws due to free speech concerns.
"We'll work our way through that," the opposition leader said when asked about in the corridors of parliament.
Taylor says he's concerned it just adds another layer of red tape.
"This is an overreach. We believe in freedom of speech. Clearly [the government] don't," he said.
Key Event
'Heavy-handed censorship': Hastie says instinct is to repeal digital duty of care
Andrew Hastie has declared the digital duty of care bill is "censorship", indicating a future Coalition government would repeal it.
The Liberal frontbencher tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast the legislation contains regulations that'll be difficult to execute.
"Well this bill is heavy-handed censorship and there's a conversation that we'll have but our instinct and our posture will be to repeal it," he tells ABC Radio National Breakfast.
The bill puts the onus on big tech companies to prevent foreseeable harms online. It's set to pass the parliament later today after the government struck a deal with the Greens.
Wells worried future Coalition government would repeal digital duty of care
A deal with the Greens means the digital duty of care legislation will be the first online safety laws to pass the parliament without bipartisan support.
So how concerned is the communications minister about them being repealed by a future Coalition government?

"It worries me. This is seismic reform but it's also reform I genuinely believe in two, five, 10 years' time we'll look back and think, 'Oh why on earth did we not regulate the industry sooner?'" she tells ABC Radio National Breakfast.

One Nation has already declared it would repeal the bill if it is elected to government. Wells notes she doesn't know if, when someone like Nationals leader Matt Canavan says they'll repeal the bill, he means the Nats or the Coalition.
Meeting with US ambassador 'really useful', Wells says
Anika Wells briefed US ambassador David Brat before she unveiled the government's deal on the digital duty of care bill.
The bill puts the onus on big tech companies to prevent foreseeable harms online.

The ambassador raised objections to the legislation, raising concerns about the definition of harms, penalties for social media platforms and whether it would "push platforms to censor lawful speech".
Wells declines to "hypothesise" about how the Trump administration will respond.
"It was our first meeting together. It was really useful," she tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast of the meeting with Brat.

"I think we both understand each other's positions and we're ironing out where there are points of difference. Like I said, we won't take a backward step from protecting Australian kids and helping Australian parents, and they won't take a backward step from their position."
What will be the benchmark for success for the digital duty of care?
Communications Minister Anika Wells is on a victory lap of sorts this morning, ahead of the passage of the digital duty of care bill today.
Labor reached a deal with the Greens to pass its the legislation today, agreeing to a series of amendments to increase penalties and give people greater power to hold tech giants to account.
So what will be Wells's benchmark for success for the laws in a year from now?
"Digital platforms taking responsibility for the harms they have built and the digital platforms being culpable where that harm has hurt Australians," she tells ABC Radio National Breakfast.
Asked how the government will ensure the tech companies pay fines, Wells points to Canada and the European Union, which also have financial penalties in place.
As part of the deal, Australians will be granted the right to sue the platforms. But Wells thinks that would be a pretty rare outcome.
Key Event
Taylor welcomes Solomon Islands scrapping China security pact
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has welcomed the Solomon Islands scrapping its pact with China.
The ABC confirmed Honiara won't renew the agreement, signed back in 2022, when it expires in April next year. The deal was signed in the weeks leading up to the 2022 federal election.
Solomon Islands PM Matthew Wale is in Canberra today, where he's expected to sign a sweeping treaty with Australia.

Taylor is asked by ABC's News Breakfast how a Coalition government would stop a such a deal with China being signed in the future. The opposition leader notes the change of leadership in the Solomon Islands.

"You have to keep investing in them, there's no doubt about that. That's incredibly important. But it also depends on who's leading these countries too. And we have seen a change in leadership there," he says."That's important. And what we're seeing [is] the results of that now. And that is a good thing."

"You have to keep investing in them, there's no doubt about that. That's incredibly important. But it also depends on who's leading these countries too. And we have seen a change in leadership there," he says.
"That's important. And what we're seeing [is] the results of that now. And that is a good thing."
'We've got to be ready': Taylor tells team to prepare for election
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor was out and about bright and early this morning, stopping by the ABC News Breakfast studio.

He was asked about a speech he gave yesterday to his troops, rallying MPs to get ready for an early election they could win thanks to rising government unpopularity and challenging economic conditions.
"We've got to be ready because the country is heading in the wrong direction," he says.
"Everything is heading in the wrong direction. Interest rates up, inflation up, unemployment up, spending up, taxation up. Real wages are down and standard of living is down.

"And we've got inflation data coming out today. The expectation is it will continue to be high. It's expected to be up. and this is pain that Australians are feeling every day. So we've got to be ready to change our rotten government and fix our country, which is heading in the wrong direction."
Former Treasury head Martin Parkinson to call for cap on temporary visa holders
Former Treasury secretary Martin Parkinson will call for a cap on the number of temporary visa holders in Australia or a limit on how long people can remain on temporary visas.
Parkinson, who led the Albanese government's 2023 migration review, will warn that cutting migration numbers alone will not restore public trust.
He has also renewed his call for a national migration summit, urging governments to tie migration settings to housing and infrastructure delivery.

"I am not against limits. A cap or a time limit is right if it comes from a decision about what each visa is for. It is wrong if it comes from a target," he will say in prepared remarks for a Macquarie Business School forum in Sydney.

Key Event
Solomon Islands PM welcomed to Canberra ahead of expected treaty
Australia is on the cusp of signing a major new treaty with Solomon Islands as the Pacific nation's prime minister visits Canberra this morning.
Matthew Wale will receive a ceremonial welcome at Parliament House at 9am before sitting down for formal meetings with Anthony Albanese.
After that the two leaders will put pen to paper and sign a "comprehensive" economic and security treaty, which has been negotiated with lightning speed.
Wale's office said last night the signing will "mark an important milestone in strengthening the longstanding partnership between the two countries".
Around 20 Solomon Islands MPs (almost half the parliament) are heading to Australia for the ceremony, so there will likely be plenty of pomp.

The deal is expected to enshrine Australia's position as Solomon Islands's key security partner. Most observers expect Canberra will also secure commitments which give it a say over some national security decisions in Solomon Islands — comparable to those found in its agreements with other pacific nations like Vanuatu, Tuvalu and Fiji.

In return, Australia is expected to substantially boost its support to Honiara, with hundreds of millions of dollars due to be ploughed into the government's key economic, education and development priorities over coming years.
Greens to demand inquiry into Labor's Working Holiday Maker visa changes
The Greens want to establish an inquiry into Labor's recent Working Holiday Maker (WHM) visa changes.
Last week, Labor backed down on its planned overhaul of the working holiday-maker program, agreeing to increase the third-year visas from 5,000 to 25,000.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke confirmed that holiday-makers would need to complete 120 days of regional work, up from 88 days, to quality for a second-year visa.

The scope of proposed inquiry includes examining how the changes would impact agriculture and tourism, Australia's reliance on WHM to fill labour shortages, review the reason behind delays in processing times for WHM and find out who was consulted about the changes.
Greens agriculture and tourism spokesperson senator Vanessa Bleyer says the changes will send "shockwaves through regional Australia".

"We need to know why this government saw fit to announce these changes without consulting key stakeholders, and how industries can be shielded from similar policies in the future," she says."Backpackers are tourists not migrants, and Labor has unfairly singled them out as it joins One Nation in a race to the bottom on migration."

Public service could face spending cuts in MYEFO
Treasurer Jim Chalmers has nominated the public service as an area that may face spending cuts in next month's budget update.

Speaking to 7.30 last night, Chalmers reiterated promises that the Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook (MYEFO) will feature savings, as the government prepares for inflation to rise again as the ABS releases its latest figures today.
"We're looking in a number of areas, the savings won't be concentrated in one portfolio or another," he said.
"Obviously we'll have to look at the efficiency of the public service, and in other areas as well, we've made that clear".
The ABC understands the cuts could include public service contractors, but Chalmers says the government is "looking right across the board".
He says the government has saved more than it has spent in all eight of its budgets, and will do so again in the ninth.
